sentence.text: Over 2027–2031, Pennsylvania would likely permit between 2,500 and 12,000 more homes (2.3–8.6%) with development fees cut in half, on top of a baseline of 67,000–180,000 homes expected under today's rules.

label.text: Baseline: homes permitted under today's rules
Homes added by the reforms
Change from the baseline

why.text: Middle estimate: 4.9% more homes than the baseline. “Adds some” means 1% to under 5%.

label.text: Fee saving per unit

meaning.text: How much the fee cut saves a builder on each new home.

steps.formula: Development fees per unit, all major categories ($50,000/unit) × Cut applied to every fee category (0.5) = $25,000/unit

label.text: Baseline units 2027-2031, building types reached

meaning.text: Homes the baseline expects to be permitted in the building types this reform reaches.

steps.formula: baseline units 2027-2031 in the building types this reform reaches = 141,660 units (projected from building permits)

label.text: Value per new unit

meaning.text: What a typical new home is worth, so the saving can be compared with it.

steps.formula: value per new unit, effective = average saving / baseline-weighted average of (saving / value) over counties and building types = $259,449/unit (county medians from ACS brackets x (1 + new-construction premium); rented types capitalised at the cap rate)

label.text: Saving as a share of value

meaning.text: The saving as a share of a new home's value: the size of the push to build.

steps.formula: fee saving per unit ($25,000/unit) ÷ value per new unit (effective) ($259,449/unit) = 0.0964

label.text: Medium-run supply response to a change in profit per unit

meaning.text: How strongly builders respond when building becomes more profitable.

steps.formula: Medium-run supply response to a change in profit per unit = 1 (ledger supply.elasticity_medium_run, central)

label.text: Share of a fee cut that reaches the decision to build

meaning.text: How much of the fee cut reaches the decision to build, rather than land prices.

general.title: What these estimates cannot tell you

items.text: These are likely ranges of building permits, not a forecast of homes finished.
They describe the whole state. They do not say which lots, streets or owners would build.
They do not say who would live in the new homes or what they would pay.
They assume every town follows the new rule from the first day and approves permits at today's pace.
They say nothing about years after the five-year period.
The baseline repeats recent permit trends under today's rules. It does not predict a recession or a boom.
Counties without a permit office, or with imputed permit counts, carry the Census Bureau's estimates.
Whether towns would replace lost fee revenue with other charges.
Whether roads, pipes or schools paid for by fees would be delayed, which could slow building.
How the saving is shared between landowners, builders and buyers in any one place.

title.text: How many more homes would Pennsylvania permit?

label.text: More homes permitted with the reforms
Baseline: homes permitted under today's rules
With the reforms

body.text: Over 2027–2031, Pennsylvania would likely permit between 2,500 and 12,000 more homes (2.3–8.6%) with development fees cut in half, on top of a baseline of 67,000–180,000 homes expected under today's rules.
Decision support, not a forecast. Not an official state document.

meaning.text: Extra homes from the fee cut, at central values.

title.text: What these estimates cannot tell you

label.text: More homes permitted with the reforms

body.text: These are likely ranges of building permits, not a forecast of homes finished.
They describe the whole state. They do not say which lots, streets or owners would build.
They do not say who would live in the new homes or what they would pay.
They assume every town follows the new rule from the first day and approves permits at today's pace.
They say nothing about years after the five-year period.
Decision support, not a forecast. Not an official state document.
